 _KABUL, Afghanistan - _On the morning of Nov. 13, 2001, Abdul Maruf Ahmadi
was a teenager standing on a street in Kabul, watching men shave off their
beards. The Taliban had slipped out of the capital overnight after they were
overthrown by the invading Americans and their Afghan allies. By dawn, the
fighters of the so-called Northern Alliance were rolling in on pickup trucks,
and music, banned for five years, was playing again from shopfronts. People
cheered. Women who had been confined to their homes stepped outside and threw
away their burqas.

"For many people, it was a relief. They have had enough of the repressions,"
Ahmadi told me when I met him in Kabul this autumn. He is in his early 40s
now, and he does not romanticize the Taliban, then or now. But he remembers
how quickly the joy curdled.

Within days, Kabul and [the rest of the country became a hunting
ground](https://www.hrw.org/report/2004/03/08/enduring-freedom/abuses-us-
forces-afghanistan). American aircraft [dropped
leaflets](http://com/2001/10/16/world/nation-challenged-propaganda-us-steps-
up-leaflets-radio-broa) promising "wealth and power beyond your dreams" to
anyone who handed over Taliban or al-Qaeda fighters. Men who had been nobody
the week before picked up rifles and became bounty hunters. Anyone could be a
"suspect": a former Taliban conscript, a rival in a land dispute, a stranger
with the wrong accent or the wrong beard. "Suddenly, everyone who spoke Pashto
[the dominant language within the Taliban] became suspicious, also men who
wore beards and turbans," Ahmadi, a Tajik and native of Kabul, said.

A 2006 study by[ Seton Hall University's law
school](https://law.shu.edu/center-policy-research/guantanamo-reports.html) of
the Pentagon's own records on Guantanamo detainees found that only a small
fraction had been captured by U.S. forces. The large majority had been handed
over by Pakistani authorities or the Northern Alliance, at a time when the US
was paying bounties. In the north, forces loyal to the warlord Abdul Rashid
Dostum packed surrendered Taliban prisoners into sealed shipping containers.
Hundreds, perhaps thousands, suffocated or were shot on the way to Sheberghan
prison, and[ were buried in the desert at Dasht-e-
Leili.](https://phr.org/issues/investigating-deaths-and-mass-
atrocities/assessments-and-documentation-of-mass-crimes/assessments-in-
afghanistan/assessments-in-afghanistan-dasht-e-leili-photos/)

This is the part of the story the anniversary leaves out. The fall of Kabul
was sold as a liberation, and for many Kabulis that morning it felt like one.
But Washington and its NATO allies did not hand Afghanistan to the people, to
ordinary Afghans. It handed it back to the warlords whose civil war made the
rise of the Taliban possible in the first place, and then spent two decades
and well over $100 billion to keep them in power. What followed was a grim
"War on Terror" that filled the dungeons of Bagram with the tortured and the
innocent, an allegedly democratic state hollowed out by plunder, and a Taliban
insurgency fed by both. Now the Taliban are back and the warlords are in
exile, and many Afghans fear the same cycle of conquest and revenge is about
to happen once more.
